clinicalPearls: A triad of vascularising keratitis, ichthyosiform (often erythrokeratodermic) skin, and congenital sensorineural deafness
Skin shows thickened, leathery, verrucous or spiky hyperkeratotic plaques, characteristically with well-demarcated 'stippled' or reticulated palmoplantar keratoderma
Progressive corneal neovascularisation and keratitis threaten vision and often worsen over time
Caused by dominant mutations in GJB2 encoding the gap-junction protein connexin 26, which also underlies non-syndromic deafness
Increased susceptibility to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and bacterial skin infection, and a lifelong risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Follicular occlusion, alopecia, dystrophic nails and dental abnormalities are common associated features
Management is largely supportive with emollients/keratolytics, meticulous skin and eye care, infection surveillance and audiological/ophthalmological input
reference.pathophysiology: KID syndrome results from usually dominant, often de novo mutations in GJB2, the gene encoding connexin 26. Connexins assemble into gap-junction channels that allow direct intercellular exchange of small molecules and ions; the disease-causing mutations act in a dominant fashion that disturbs channel gating and epidermal and cochlear cell communication. The resulting defect impairs epidermal differentiation and keratinocyte homeostasis, producing hyperkeratosis and a compromised barrier, disrupts inner-ear function causing sensorineural deafness, and affects the corneal epithelium leading to keratitis with neovascularisation. Impaired barrier and immune function predispose to infection and, over time, to keratinocyte malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma / other congenital ichthyoses
HID (hystrix-like ichthyosis-deafness) syndrome, an allelic variant
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis
Molecular genetic testing for GJB2 (connexin 26) mutations
Audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Ophthalmological (slit-lamp) examination for keratitis and corneal neovascularisation
Microbiological swabs/cultures for candidal and bacterial superinfection
Periodic dermatological surveillance and biopsy of suspicious hyperkeratotic or ulcerated lesions
redFlags: New, enlarging, ulcerated or non-healing hyperkeratotic lesion suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Progressive corneal opacification or neovascularisation with visual deterioration
Recurrent or invasive candidal or bacterial infection
Rapidly extending erythroderma with barrier failure in infancy
reference.prognosis: KID syndrome is a lifelong, progressive condition; vision may deteriorate from keratitis and deafness is usually permanent. The most serious long-term concern is a substantially increased risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, so continued surveillance is essential.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent skin or mucosal infection to poor hygiene rather than the intrinsic immune/barrier defect
Overlooking malignant transformation within chronic hyperkeratotic plaques
Assuming systemic retinoids will reliably help, as response is variable and they may aggravate keratitis
Missing the diagnosis when the deafness or ocular features precede overt skin change
